text: Data Governance Foundations covered the roadmap a brand-new program needs to get off the ground — discovery, foundation, pilot, expand, scale, over about a year. This lesson picks up after that: the program is already running, so what does year two's roadmap actually look like?

A first-program roadmap is mostly linear, because foundation has to come before pilot. A sustaining roadmap is different — it's a backlog of competing initiatives, all wanting the same limited stewardship and council time, re-sorted on a regular cadence instead of following one fixed calendar.

Mature programs sort that backlog into three horizons. Now: committed work this quarter, with a named owner and milestone. Next: likely work for the following one to two quarters, scoped but not yet committed. Later: real candidates, described loosely on purpose, so the roadmap never pretends to know things it doesn't know yet.

Four things legitimately reshuffle a mature roadmap: a maturity assessment exposing a weak dimension, a new domain or regulation forcing urgent work to the front, a funding change that forces re-ranking by value, and stakeholder turnover stalling work that depended on one person's momentum.

Keep it honest the same way Foundations taught for a first roadmap, just at a longer time scale: revisit every horizon on a fixed cadence, retire items the evidence no longer supports, and show what actually moved to done last quarter — not just what's planned next. Next: funding and business cases for a program that already exists.
